parole.significato: A religion icon (chiefly of Christ or the Virgin Mary) believed not to have been created by human hands; a miraculous i…
parole.testo: From Byzantine Greek ἀχειροποίητον (akheiropoíēton), from ἀ- (a-, “a-, the alpha privative”) + χείρ (kheír, “hand”) + ποιεῖν (poieîn, “to make”).

parole.significato: A type of javelin with a barbed tip, used by the Franks and the various Germanic tribes in the Late Antiquity and Early…
parole.testo: From Byzantine Greek ἄγγων (ángōn, “prong, hook”); ultimately of Gothic *𐌰𐌲𐌲𐌰 (*agga, “prong, hook”) and that from Proto-Germanic *angô (“hook; barb; angle”).

parole.significato: A piece of ordinary leavened bread, taken from remnants of loaves used for the Eucharist, which has been blessed but no…
parole.testo: From Byzantine Greek αντίδωρον (antídōron) from Koine Greek ἀντίδωρον (antídōron) from Ancient Greek ἀντί + δῶρον (antí + dôron, “gift in return; instead of a gift”).

parole.significato: A member of a population group in Greece who traditionally speak Arvanitika, a dialect of Albanian, and who settled in…
parole.testo: Ultimately from Byzantine Greek Ἀρβανίτης (Arbanítēs), a variant of Ἀλβανίτης (Albanítēs, “Albanian”), possibly influenced by the Modern Greek reading of β (v).

parole.significato: A composition used in Orthodox Christianity to create other hymns, following its melody and rhythm.
parole.testo: From Byzantine Greek αὐτόμελον (autómelon), neuter of αὐτόμελος, from Ancient Greek αὐτός (autós) + μέλος

parole.significato: A type of padded under-garment, worn under armour, especially by Byzantine troops.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Byzantine Greek βαμβάκιον (bambákion).

parole.significato: Synonym of Byzantine.
parole.testo: From Byzantine Greek Βῡζᾰντῐᾰκός (Būzăntĭăkós), in some uses perhaps via Greek Βυζαντιακός (Vyzantiakós).

parole.significato: The governor of a catepanate such as the Catepanate of Italy, a Byzantine province.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Byzantine Greek κατεπάνω (katepánō, literally “[the one] placed at the top, or the topmost”).

parole.significato: A respiratory system, in the form of a comb, in some molluscs
parole.testo: Borrowed from Byzantine Greek κτενίδιον (ktenídion, “comb”). By surface analysis, cteno- + -idium.

parole.significato: A cuff worn over the sticharion by clergy in the Greek Orthodox Church, corresponding to a maniple in other Catholic ch…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Byzantine Greek ἐπιμανίκιον (epimaníkion), from ἐπί (epí, “upon”) + μανίκιον (maníkion, “sleeve”).

parole.significato: An insignia or some other distinguishing symbol.
parole.testo: From Byzantine Greek ἐπίσημον (epísēmon), from Ancient Greek ἐπίσημος (epísēmos, “distinguished; remarkable”), from ἐπί (epí, “above”) + σῆμα (sêma, “sign”).

parole.significato: The liturgical vestment worn by priests and bishops of the Eastern Orthodox Church as the symbol of their priesthood, c…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Byzantine Greek ἐπιτραχήλιον (epitrakhḗlion), from Ancient Greek ἐπιτραχήλιος (epitrakhḗlios, “on the neck”) + -ιον (-ion, suffix forming diminutive nouns). ἐπιτραχήλιος (epitrakhḗlios) is from ἐπι- (epi-, “on, upon, on top of, covering”) (from Proto-Indo-European *h₁epi (“on; at; near

parole.significato: The final section of a document, often involving a formulaic close (e.g. “Yours faithfully”), the date and location of…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Byzantine Greek ἔσχατοκολλον (éskhatokollon, “last sheet glued onto a manuscript”), from ἔσχατον (éskhaton) + κόλλα (kólla, “glue”).

parole.significato: A fylfot or swastika.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Byzantine Greek γαμμάδιον (gammádion), diminutive of γάμμα (gámma), after the resemblance of each of the symbol’s arms to the Greek letter gamma: Γ.

parole.significato: A monk of the Eastern Church who is also a priest.
parole.testo: From Byzantine Greek ἱερομόναχος (hieromónakhos), from Ancient Greek ἱερός (hierós) + μοναχός (monakhós).

parole.significato: A liturgical book containing the daily offices of the Eastern Orthodox and Catholic churches.
parole.testo: From Byzantine Greek ὡρολόγιον (hōrológion, “book of hours”), from Ancient Greek ὥρα (hṓra, “time period, hour”) + λόγιον (lógion, “record; measuring device”), from λόγος (lógos) + -ιον (-ion). Doublet of horologe and horologium. See menologion.

parole.significato: A Byzantine coin in use during the late Middle Ages, replacing the solidus as the Byzantine Empire’s gold coinage.
parole.testo: From Byzantine Greek ὑπέρπυρον (hupérpuron). Doublet of perper and perpera.

parole.significato: A wall of icons between the sanctuary and the nave in an Eastern Orthodox church.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Byzantine Greek εἰκονόστασις (eikonóstasis), from εἰκών (eikṓn, “icon”) + στάσις (stásis, “fixture”).

parole.significato: Accompanying drone in Byzantine music.
parole.testo: From Byzantine Greek ἴσον (íson).

parole.significato: A division of the psalter, used by Eastern Orthodox Christians and Eastern Catholics who follow the Byzantine Rite.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Byzantine Greek κάθισμα (káthisma, “a seat”).

parole.significato: A form of hymn or poem recited as a dialogue between a chanter and the choir.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Byzantine Greek κοντάκιον (kontákion).

parole.significato: often Mandylion: the Image of Edessa, a holy relic consisting of a piece of cloth upon which an image of the face of Je…
parole.testo: From Byzantine Greek μανδύλιον (mandúlion), μανδίλιον (mandílion), μαντίλιον (mantílion), or μανδήλη (mandḗlē, “cloth, hand towel, handkerchief, tablecloth”) (the last word dating to the 5th century), especially in the term τὸ ἄγιον μανδήλιον (tò ágion mandḗlion, “the holy towel”); from Latin mantēl

parole.significato: The commander-in-chief of the Byzantine navy.
parole.testo: From Byzantine Greek μέγας δούξ (mégas doúx, literally “great leader”). By surface analysis, mega- + duke.

parole.significato: A stylized date used for certain documents of the Byzantine Empire.
parole.testo: From Byzantine Greek μηνολόγημα (mēnológēma).

parole.significato: Synonym of menologium, particularly in Greek, Byzantine, and Eastern Orthodox contexts.
parole.testo: From Byzantine Greek μηνολόγιον (mēnológion), from Ancient Greek μήν (mḗn, “month”) + -ο- (-o-, “-o-”) + λόγιον (lógion, “writing, record, announcement”), from λόγος (lógos, “writing, recording”) + -ιον (-ion, “-ion: forming related nouns”). Doublet of menologe, menologium, and menology. See horolog

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Miaphysitism; maintaining that Christ has a single, though composite, nature.
parole.testo: A modern coinage from Byzantine Greek μία (mía, “one”) + φύσις (phúsis, “nature, substance”) + -ite; see Miaphysitism for more.

parole.significato: A Christological formula, upheld by the Oriental Orthodox Church, holding that divinity and humanity are united in a si…
parole.testo: From miaphysite + -ism, a modern coinage from Byzantine Greek μία (mía, “one”) + φύσις (phúsis, “nature, substance”), referring in particular to the formula of Cyril of Alexandria, “one incarnate nature of the Word”, μία φύσις τοῦ Λόγου σεσαρκωμένη (mía phúsis toû Lógou sesarkōménē).

parole.significato: A Christological doctrine, generally considered heterodox or heretical, holding that Jesus Christ has a single nature,…
parole.testo: From Byzantine Greek μονοφυσιτισμός (monophusitismós), from μόνος (mónos, “only one”) + φύσις (phúsis, “nature”) + -ισμός (-ismós, “-ism”), hence “belief in a single nature”.

parole.significato: Someone who believed Christ had two natures (human and divine), but one single will; a Monothelite.
parole.testo: Variant form of Monothelite after its etymon, Byzantine Greek μονοθελήτης (monothelḗtēs).

parole.significato: A saint whose relics or place of burial are said to have produced the Oil of Saints ("an aromatic liquid with healing p…
parole.testo: From Byzantine Greek μυροβλύτης (muroblútēs, “myron-gushing”), from the ancient μῠ́ρ(ον) (múron) + -ο- (infix) + the Hellenistic verb βλύ(ζω) (blúzō) + -της (-tēs).

parole.significato: A band of brocade originally of wool decorated with crosses and worn on the neck and around the shoulders as the distin…
parole.testo: From Byzantine Greek ὠμοφόριον (ōmophórion), from Ancient Greek ὦμος (ômos, “shoulder”) + φέρω (phérō, “carry”).

parole.significato: A Hesychast.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Byzantine Greek ὀμφαλοψυχίτης (omphalopsukhítēs), from ὀμφαλός (omphalós, “navel”) + ψυχή (psukhḗ, “soul”) + -ίτης (-ítēs, “-ite”), i.e. “one with his soul in his navel”, referring to the practice by some Hesychasts of gazing on the navel as a means to concentrate during meditation. By

parole.significato: An opponent of onomatodoxy.
parole.testo: From onomato- (back-formation from onomatodoxy) + -clast, by analogy with iconoclast, from Byzantine Greek κλάω (kláō, “to break”).

parole.significato: A follower of Paulicianism.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Byzantine Greek Παυλικιανός (Paulikianós), from Παῦλος (Paûlos) + -ικός (-ikós) + -ιανός (-ianós), originally most likely in reference to Paul the Apostle, who was held in special esteem by the group. Byzantine heresiologists conventionally traced the term to Paul of Samosata, however,

parole.significato: Eating, feeding, consuming.
parole.testo: From Byzantine Greek φᾰγ- (phăg-), perfective stem of ἔφᾰγον (éphăgon, “I ate, I devoured”), singular first-person aorist active indicative form (by suppletion) of ἐσθῐ́ω (esthĭ́ō, “to eat, devour, consume”).

parole.significato: A ritual sprinkler used in some Christian rites.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Byzantine Greek ῥαντιστήριον (rhantistḗrion), from ῥαντίζω (rhantízō) (a late form of ῥαίνω (rhaínō, “to sprinkle, purify”), from Proto-Indo-European *weri) + -ῐον (-ĭon, “suffix forming diminutive nouns”).

parole.significato: Synonym of Rhomaian; of or pertaining to the Eastern Roman (or Byzantine) empire.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Byzantine Greek Ῥωμαῖος (Rhōmaîos), referring to the autonym used by Grecophone writers in the Eastern Roman (or Byzantine) Empire.

parole.significato: A richly decorated vestment worn by Orthodox bishops, instead of a priest's phelonion (chasuble in western church).
parole.testo: From Byzantine Greek σάκκος (sákkos). Doublet of sac, saccus, sack, and saco.

parole.significato: A person holding a senior court title in the late Byzantine Empire and nearby states, generally restricted to members o…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Byzantine Greek σεβαστοκράτωρ (sebastokrátōr).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a stauropegion.
parole.testo: From Byzantine Greek σταυροπηγία (stauropēgía), from σταυρός (staurós, “cross”) (Greek σταυρός (stavrós)) + πήγνυμι (pḗgnumi, “secure, fix, fasten”).

parole.significato: In Eastern Orthodoxy, the placement of a cross by a bishop which symbolises his approval of the construction of a churc…
parole.testo: From Byzantine Greek σταυροπήγιον (stauropḗgion). See also stauropegial.

parole.significato: A ligature of the Greek letters sigma and tau: Ϛ / ϛ.
parole.testo: From Byzantine Greek στίγμα (stígma), likely coined by analogy with σίγμα (sígma).

parole.significato: A Greek unit of land area, now equal to a decare (1,000 m²) but (historical) previously 10,000 square Greek feet.
parole.testo: From Byzantine Greek στρέμμα (strémma, “a turning”), referring to the turning of the soil.

parole.significato: A specially summoned council or assembly of elders in classical Greece.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Byzantine Greek σῠ́γκλητος (sŭ́nklētos). By surface analysis, syn- (“with, together”) + Byzantine Greek κλητός (klētós, “called”).

parole.significato: Relating to the Quinisext Council held in 692 in the dome-roofed hall in the imperial palace at Constantinople.
parole.testo: From Byzantine Greek τρούλλος (troúllos, “a dome”), from Latin trulla (“a ladle”), in reference to the domed hall of the palace in Constantinople in which the council was held.

parole.significato: A mounted archer locally recruited by the Christian states during the Crusades.
parole.testo: From Byzantine Greek τουρκόπουλοι (tourkópouloi, “sons of Turks”), from Τοῦρκος (Toûrkos) + -πουλος (-poulos).

parole.significato: A member of the ethnically Scandinavian people around the borders of Constantinople in the ninth and tenth centuries.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Byzantine Greek Βάραγγος (Bárangos), from Medieval Latin Varingus, from Old Norse væringr, from várr (“pledge”) or værr (“pledge”), which is cognate with Old English wǣr (“fidelity, loyalty”), + Old Norse gangi (“companion”). Cognate with Old English wærgenga.

parole.significato: (A pair of) baggy breeches worn in the Balkans, the Greek islands (especially Crete) and in Cyprus chiefly by men but a…
parole.testo: Transliteration of Greek βράκα (vráka), from Byzantine Greek βράκα (bráka), a singular feminine noun from the Hellenistic plural of Koine Greek βράκες (brákes), from Latin brācae (singular brāca). Doublet of breech.

parole.significato: the hot water added to the chalice by the priest during the Byzantine Eucharist to commemorate the water that flowed fr…
parole.testo: From Byzantine Greek ζέον (zéon, “zeon; boiling”), from Ancient Greek ζέω (zéō, “boil”).

parole.significato: A member of the national cavalry of Hungary, Croatia and Poland.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French hussard, from Hungarian huszár (“cavalryman”), from Serbo-Croatian gusar (“corsair”), from Byzantine Greek χωσάριος, χονσάριος (khōsários, khonsários) or from Italian corsaro (“corsair”), from Medieval Latin cursārius (“pirate”), from Latin cursus (“running”), from currō (“run”)

parole.significato: Chic, fashionable, stylish; in the manner of a macaroni.
parole.testo: From Italian maccaroni (plural of maccarone (archaic variant of maccheroni (“fool”))), of uncertain origin. parole.significato: A native of Malabar.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic مَلَبَار (malabār), first attested in the writings of Iranian scholar Al-Biruni (c. 11th century). parole.significato: Cereal plants, Oryza sativa of the grass family whose seeds are used as food.
parole.testo: From Middle English rys, from Old French ris, from Old Italian riso, risi, from Byzantine Greek ὄρυζα (óruza), from an Eastern Iranian language related to Middle Persian blnc (*brinǰ), Northern Kurdish riz (beyond Euphrates) and Zazaki riz. Theorized to have come to Iranian languages from Sanskrit व

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; Probably; perhaps; or from; modello unc/uncertain
parole.significato: The probability of a negative outcome to a decision or event.
parole.testo: From earlier risque, from Middle French risque, from Old Italian risco (“risk”) (modern Italian rischio) and rischiare (“to run into danger”).
